segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for forty days, being tested by the devil. He ate nothing during those days, and when they were over he was hungry.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The devil said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to become bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘A person shall not live on bread alone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the devil led him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “To you I will give all this authority and their glory, for it has been handed over to me, and I give it to whomever I wish.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So if you worship before me, it will all be yours.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he brought him to Jerusalem, set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: for it is written: ‘He will command his angels concerning you, to guard you,’

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: and: ‘On their hands they will lift you up, so that you do not strike your foot against a stone.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It has been said: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the devil had finished every test, he withdrew from him until an opportune time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and news about him went out through the whole surrounding region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was teaching in their synagogues and was praised by everyone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and as was his custom he went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day. He stood up to read,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. Unrolling the scroll, he found the place where it was written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to bring good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim release to captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to send the oppressed away released,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he rolled up the scroll, gave it back to the attendant, and sat down. The eyes of everyone in the synagogue were fixed on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He began by saying to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone spoke well of him and marveled at the gracious words coming from his mouth, and they said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Is this not Joseph’s son?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “No doubt you will quote me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself! What we have heard happened in Capernaum, do here in your hometown as well.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, no prophet finds favor in his hometown.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you in truth, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when the sky was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came over the whole land,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: yet Elijah was sent to none of them, only to a widow at Zarephath in the region of Sidon.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And there were many people with skin disease in Israel in the time of the prophet Elisha, yet none of them was cleansed, only Naaman the Syrian.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone in the synagogue was filled with rage on hearing this.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They got up, drove him out of the town, and led him to the brow of the hill on which their town was built, intending to throw him off the cliff.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he passed through the middle of them and went on his way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went down to Capernaum, a town in Galilee, and was teaching them on the Sabbath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were astounded at his teaching, because his word carried authority.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the synagogue there was a man who had the spirit of an unclean demon, and he cried out in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Ha! What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus rebuked him, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Be silent, and come out of him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The demon threw the man down in their midst and came out of him without doing him any harm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Amazement came over them all, and they said to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What is this word? For with authority and power he commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And talk about him spread to every place in the surrounding region.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He left the synagogue and went into Simon’s house. Simon’s mother-in-law was suffering from a high fever, and they asked him to help her.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and it left her. At once she got up and began to serve them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As the sun was setting, all who had people sick with various diseases brought them to him, and he laid his hands on each one of them and healed them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Demons also came out of many, shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are the Son of God!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he rebuked them and would not let them speak, because they knew that he was the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When day came, he went out and made his way to a deserted place. The crowds were looking for him, and when they reached him they tried to keep him from leaving them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I must bring the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is what I was sent for.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he went on proclaiming in the synagogues of Judea.

notes.note: The Greek verb means to put to the test, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the regular word for Israel’s testing in the wilderness, the story from which all three of Jesus’ replies are drawn. Modern “tempt” has narrowed to enticement to sin, which hides that link. Most translations keep “tempted” here, though some recent versions and many commentators prefer “tested”; lexicons recognize both senses.

Luke does not use the general word for “world” found in Matthew’s parallel but a term for the inhabited earth, which in everyday usage often meant the Roman empire (as in Luke 2:1). Most translations simply have “world.” A first-century reader would have heard a political ring in the offer of these kingdoms.

This is the ordinary Greek verb for transferring a person or thing into someone else’s control, and this translation renders it “hand over” wherever it has that sense so the reader can follow the word through the Gospel. The passive leaves unstated who did the handing over. The claim is the devil’s own, and the narrative does not vouch for it.

The Greek word denotes a projecting tip or edge, and it is not known which part of the temple complex is meant. Suggestions include the southeast corner of the outer wall above the Kidron valley and the roof edge of the sanctuary itself. The traditional “pinnacle” is kept as a neutral term for a high point.

The noun belongs with the verb rendered “tested” in verse 2 and means a putting to the proof. Most translations have “temptation” here; “test” keeps the connection with the verb and with the wilderness background.

The Greek verb was an ordinary word for announcing good news, used also of public and royal proclamations. “Gospel” is now a religious term or the name of a book, so “good news” is used here; many modern translations do the same.

notes.traditional: set at liberty those who are oppressed
notes.note: The reading combines Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from Isaiah 58:6, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. The noun translated “release” occurs twice; in the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the release of debts and slaves in the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25), and elsewhere in Luke it is the usual word for forgiveness of sins. The rendering keeps both the repeated “release” and the echo between “sent me” and “send.”

The Greek says literally that all “were bearing witness to him,” which most interpreters take as approval. A minority reads it as testifying against him, in view of how quickly the mood turns hostile. In the same way, “gracious words” could mean words about God’s grace, and the question about Joseph’s son can be heard as admiring or as dismissive.

The Greek adjective is the same one used in verse 19 for the year of the Lord’s favor. Most translations have “accepted” or “welcome” here and so lose the echo. The rendering keeps it: the town that hears the year of the Lord’s favor announced shows no favor to the prophet who announces it.
The same Greek word covers both the visible sky and God’s dwelling. Here the reference is to the drought in Elijah’s time (1 Kings 17–18), so “sky” is used, as in several modern translations.

The Greek word names those with the condition regulated in Leviticus 13–14, a range of scaly skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean, which is why Naaman is said to be “cleansed.” “Leper” today means someone with Hansen’s disease, which is narrower than the biblical term and may not even be included in it. Most translations keep “lepers,” usually with a footnote saying as much.

The Greek is either an exclamation of surprise or displeasure, or the imperative of a verb meaning “let, leave alone.” Translations are divided between “Ha!” or “Ah!” and “Let us alone!” Either fits the scene.

Here the Greek word is a title, the anointed king Israel expected, and not yet a name for Jesus. “Messiah” conveys the title as a first-century Jewish hearer would have heard it. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where the word works as a name.

Many manuscripts read “Galilee,” which matches Mark 1:39 and the surrounding narrative. The earliest witnesses have “Judea,” and most editors judge that scribes changed it to “Galilee” to remove the difficulty. Luke sometimes uses “Judea” for the whole land of the Jews, Galilee included, and that may be the sense here.

candidates.reason: The same noun means release of captives and debts here and forgiveness of sins elsewhere, and readers lose Luke’s link between the two unless the renderings are coordinated.
It is distinct from the general word for world and often carries an imperial sense, so it needs one policy across Luke–Acts, Hebrews and Revelation.
Translations vary between authority, power and right, and it needs to be kept apart from the word rendered “power” when the two stand together, as in verse 36.
It is used of demons, a fever, wind and disciples; versions vary between rebuke, order sternly and warn, which hides the repeated pattern.
Traditional “preach” now suggests a sermon, and the word needs to be kept consistently distinct from the verb for bringing good news.
